# zurngtest

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zurngtest/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zurngtest/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pedrobtz/zurngtest/gh-pages/badges/coverage.svg)](https://github.com/pedrobtz/zurngtest/actions/workflows/coverage.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

## Overview

A random number generator can pass every statistical test you know of and
still fail the one that matters for your simulation. The test suite that
the current literature on generator design reports against is
[PractRand](https://pracrand.sourceforge.net/), by Chris Doty-Humphrey: it
tests a stream of bits at doubling lengths and reports the length at which
a generator first fails. Until now, using it from R meant writing bytes to
a file and running its command-line tool.

zurngtest runs PractRand from R:

* **PractRand's own verdicts.** The core and expanded batteries of
  PractRand 0.96, with its labels and thresholds unchanged. With the core
  battery, `pract_test()` gives the results PractRand's own `RNG_test`
  gives for the same bytes, which a continuous-integration job checks.
* **R's generators on their own bits.** `pract_rng()` recovers the integers
  behind `runif()` for each `RNGkind()` where they exist, and leaves the
  session's random numbers as they were.
* **Any source of bits.** Raw bytes, connections, R functions, and
  combinations of them, such as two seeds of one generator interleaved.
* **A fast path for generator packages.** Generators written in C hand
  their words to PractRand directly, at about the speed of `RNG_test`.
* **No dependencies beyond R.** PractRand is bundled, and zurngtest
  imports only base R's stats.

## Installation

zurngtest is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zurngtest")
```

## Usage

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(zurngtest)
```

The low byte of a linear congruential generator repeats every 256 values.
PractRand needs a few kilobytes to see it:

```{r}
lcg_low_bits <- local({
  x <- 1
  function(n) {
    out <- raw(n)
    for (i in seq_len(n)) {
      x <<- (1664525 * x + 1013904223) %% 2^32
      out[i] <- as.raw(x %% 256)
    }
    out
  }
})
pract_test(pract_fun(lcg_low_bits, bits = 8), min_bytes = 2^12, max_bytes = 2^14)
```

R's default generator, Mersenne-Twister, tested on its own 32-bit integers,
does not fail over the first 4 megabytes. An "unusual" result now and then
is what a good generator gives; a "FAIL" is not:

```{r}
pract_test(pract_rng("Mersenne-Twister", seed = 1), min_bytes = 2^20, max_bytes = 2^22)
```

Seeding schemes deserve testing too, since a combination of streams can
fail where each stream passes. Two seeds of Mersenne-Twister, interleaved
word by word, pass:

```{r}
seeds <- pract_interleave(pract_rng(seed = 1), pract_rng(seed = 2))
res <- pract_test(seeds, min_bytes = 2^20, max_bytes = 2^21)
```

The result is a data frame with one row per test and length, and the first
failing length, if any, in its `failed_at` attribute:

```{r}
attr(res, "failed_at")
head(as.data.frame(res), 3)
```

## Learn more

* [Testing a generator package](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zurngtest/articles/generator-packages.html):
  testing a package's generators from R and from C.
* [The reference index](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zurngtest/reference/)
  documents every function, and `?pract_test` lists PractRand's
  evaluations.

## Related work

PractRand is by Chris Doty-Humphrey and is in the public domain; zurngtest
bundles version 0.96 with a few patches, described in the package's
`src/practrand/PROVENANCE`. On CRAN, [RDieHarder](https://cran.r-project.org/package=RDieHarder)
runs the older DieHarder suite.
